title: Learning-Time Encoding Shapes Unlearning in LLMs
claim: The same piece of knowledge can be encoded in different textual forms (direct, paraphrased, or implied within longer text), which sets up the study of how encoding affects unlearning.
layout: 1 panel, top-to-bottom, three stacked text examples inside a page-curl box
description: A single rounded box with a folded page corner at the top right, holding three stacked text examples. The first is a plain textual description of a fact in monospace type: 'Reid Perry has Richard Perry as his father.' The second is a paraphrased description of the same fact: 'The father of Reid Perry is Richard Perry.' The third is a longer text chunk about Richard Perry, with a birth year, a job and a family, which implies the same fact. Bold black labels introduce each example. Red text marks the word 'implies' and the phrases in the chunk that carry the fact. There are no arrows or icons. The eye goes first to the bold labels and the red highlights.
caption: Examples of different textual descriptions for the same piece of knowledge in Eval-DU+.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in the real world, the ability to ``unlearn'', or remove specific pieces of knowledge post hoc, has become essential for a variety of reasons ranging from privacy regulations to correcting outdated or harmful content. Prior work has proposed unlearning benchmarks and algorithms, and has typically assumed that the training process and the target model are fixed. In this work, we empirically investigate how learning-time choices in knowledge encoding impact the effectiveness of unlearning factual knowledge. Our experiments reveal two key findings: (1) learning with paraphrased descriptions improves unlearning performance and (2) unlearning individual piece of knowledge from a chunk of text is challenging. Our results suggest that learning-time knowledge encoding may play a central role in enabling reliable post-hoc unlearning.
